 Shops & Markets When SNAP leaves families empty-handed, food banks become a lifeline
 The application process has become a maddening runaround. Arizonans are turning to local food pantries. 
 By Sara Crocker November 9, 2026 
 Artist and educator Jocelyn Sewell paints faces when she visits the food bank. Provided by United Food Bank

 This article is part of a package of stories featured on Phoenix New Times’ Oct. 29 cover, exploring the devastating fallout Arizona has seen after the federal government gutted food assistance last year. The cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, SNAP, benefit theft and process shortfalls have left Arizonans making hard decisions to feed their families. 
 When Jocelyn Sewell lost her job last fall, she worried about how she’d feed her family. 
 Sewell, a long-time art teacher, moved to Casa Grande from Maryland about four years ago to help open a school. She and her husband have two adult children who live with them — one who just started his career and another in college. Sewell’s husband works in manufacturing and is studying for his engineering degree.
 The artist joined the growing number of unemployed Arizonans just as the federal food stamps program was remade. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, SNAP, exists as a safety net for low- and no-income Americans, providing dollars for groceries. Sewell buys groceries for her household.

 First, she tried cutting nonessential spending. No more subscriptions or salon appointments. She gave her car to her son so that he could drive to work. She expanded her vegetable garden. But they still were struggling to afford food. 
 “Everything keeps going up,” she says.
 She applied for SNAP to see if she could get help while she looked for work. Sewell soon found herself in a confusing tangle of red tape that took months to unknot. 
 While she waited on the government, she turned to her local food bank. This year marked the first time that more Arizonans visit food banks than receive SNAP benefits.
 advertisement 
 advertisement 
 Organizations like United Food Bank , which Sewell visited, have reported double-digit increases in demand in the last year. The East Valley food bank served nearly 21% more people over the summer.
 Sewell had never previously sought public assistance. The application process became a maddening game of whack-a-mole. She waited hours in line at a Department of Economic Security office hoping to meet with a caseworker, but left only with a phone appointment.
 Sewell missed her first call from DES, as her phone screens unknown numbers. It took about six to eight weeks to connect with DES and schedule her required interview, Sewell says. 
 During the interview, she was asked to submit documents, which she’d already filed. Then she got a notice that she hadn’t filed those documents in time. Frustrated, she resubmitted the application.
 advertisement 
 During this process, Sewell still needed to put food on the table. A friend told her about one of United’s Neighbor Pantries. It became a lifeline. 
 She and her friend drove about an hour from her home and joined a long line. Once inside, she got a cart filled with food and added eggplant, spinach, squash and bread. Sewell has Type 1 diabetes. Those fresh options make a difference. 
 Over the last year, she started tutoring and face painting. It hasn’t replaced her income, but it’s helped. When she’s at the food pantry, she offers to paint kids’ faces to help families pass the time in line.
 About five months after she first applied for SNAP, Sewell finally got a letter approving her for benefits. 
 She’d get $28 a month. 
 “That can’t even fill up a tank of gas,” she says, noting that the entire process was beyond disheartening.
 “They say that these resources are available to help you get out of this situation,” Sewell says. “It makes you wonder, whoever set this up, did they do the math?”
